analysis.one_liner: Lets people wipe out private student loans in bankruptcy like credit card debt.
analysis.headline: The bill to let people erase private student loans in bankruptcy died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, almost no student loan — private or federal — can be erased in bankruptcy unless the borrower proves an 'undue hardship,' a standard courts apply so strictly that it is nearly impossible to meet. That means a family facing medical bills or job loss can shed credit card debt but not a private student loan. This bill would change the bankruptcy code so that loans from private lenders could be discharged in bankruptcy like other consumer debts, while leaving government-backed loans under the stricter rule.
analysis.who_benefits: Student borrowers holding high-cost private loans who fell into genuine hardship. They would regain the option of a bankruptcy discharge — a legal escape hatch that existed before 2005 and that applies to nearly every other kind of consumer debt. Families cosigning those loans would also be freed if the borrower's debt is erased.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Borrowers with crushing private student loans

how_it_helps.text: It amends the bankruptcy code so that privately issued student loans can be wiped out in bankruptcy like credit card debt and medical bills, instead of being dischargeable only for an 'undue hardship' that courts rarely find.
Government-backed loans would keep the stricter rule, targeting relief at borrowers who took on high-cost private loans.

analysis.who_pays: Private student lenders, who would face bankruptcy losses and may raise rates or lend more cautiously as a result.

drawbacks.text: Making private loans dischargeable could raise interest rates or tighten lending, since lenders would absorb losses from borrowers who file for bankruptcy.
The bill leaves federal and government-backed student loans under the strict undue-hardship rule, so most borrowers — whose loans are usually federal — would get little relief.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers drowning in private student debt with no way out, the change is significant: it restores a safety valve that existed before 2005 and matches how other consumer debts are treated. The cost is real but limited: lenders could charge slightly more or lend less, and government-backed loans would remain nearly impossible to discharge, so the bill helps only part of the struggling-borrower population. Weighing who bears each side — borrowers versus private lenders — the balance favors borrowers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 25, 2017, read twice, and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote, and it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student lenders keep the exceptional protection that makes student debt nearly impossible to escape, and borrowers remain stuck with the debt.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its cosponsors.

for.name: 12 Senate Democrats
for.role: Cosponsors including Warren, Whitehouse, Blumenthal, Franken, Hirono, Reed, Wyden, Baldwin, Hassan, Kaine, Murphy

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and took no action on it — no hearing, no markup, no report.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-controlled Judiciary Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: Private lenders would lose their guarantee that student debt follows a borrower for life, facing losses in bankruptcy proceedings and possibly pricing that risk into loans. Today that guarantee lets them collect long after other debts would be wiped clean.
Easier discharge of private loans could reduce how much families can borrow, potentially pressuring tuition — a modest pressure rather than a direct mandate.
